cells.tense: Right now the words are carrying their weight, and nothing in you has to strain to place them.
cells.act: teach what you feel by doing it with others
cells.ask: Do the thing you understand best beside someone who's learning it too — same session, same hour, you working in it rather than watching from the side.
cells.core:
What you're soft-spoken about is usually the truest part. Somewhere in you the pieces fit better than any sentence that carries them out, and most days that gap stays cheap. You can feel when a word does its job and when it is only being said; it comes fast, and it isn't worried about being fast. That steadiness lets you say hard things sideways and still land them, and lets a room settle without anyone announcing it.

Take the step one click smaller. Whatever you notice clearly is teachable, and you can hand it along — not as a lesson, as a tone: do it beside someone, don't tell them how. Teaching what you feel by doing it with others, once this week, small enough that nobody calls it a class. You'll know it worked if something gets clearer in both of you, and nothing about you had to get louder.

cells.tense: The future is being read before it has arrived, and the words are doing the smoothing.
cells.act: tend the fire without burning out
cells.ask: Take the stretch you've already decided and tend it smaller: a warm half hour on the part you actually enjoy, then stop while it still feels like yours.
cells.core:
You are reading a situation you are not yet in. The shape shows itself long before anyone has said anything, and lately you translate that shape into words as if it were a later page already written. It makes you steady — you stay calm in rooms because you know how the next minute goes. The cost is that the people you translate for can feel bracketed rather than met; the facts correct, the person missed. Seeing how things work is one thing. Finishing the sentence alone is another.

Underneath, something is doing the hauling, and that is what needs the smaller portion. Tend the fire without burning out — keep a short stretch warm and stop before it fades. Then speak to whoever you read too early, if there is one. What you'll have is your read on things back at eating size, honest about how much is not on the page yet.

cells.tense: There was a correct thing to say once, and it stayed up here, and behind the tongue it has been dark since.
cells.act: hold space for what someone feels without fixing it
cells.ask: Ask someone how their week's going and stay with whatever comes back — no fixing, no tidying, no advice, nothing to carry off after.
cells.core:
There is a door behind you that you are still at. You saw how it went, you saw what would have been the truest sentence, and your mouth didn't send it — so it stayed up here and the room moved on without it. In someone else's trouble you can still find the exact shape, quick as ever, and it does nothing. From outside you look far away. From inside it is a hand stuck at the length of the arm, knowing the right thing and not crossing. Being very clear and not arriving has its own flatness.

Go smaller than a confrontation. Ask someone how their week is going, and stay with the answer — nothing fixed, nothing carried off, no advice. Keep your own footing by hearing without merging. Then say one true thing of your own, if one is there.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room where the writing is already underway through you.
cells.act: make a ritual of the shared thing
cells.ask: Take something you've said that people came back to, and say it again this week as if you meant it — unshrunk, unexplained, left out where others can hear it.
cells.core:
People come to you for words you don't count. They carry off some line of yours they've kept, you watch it land, then wave it off as talking around. Your read on things is not only for the inside; it is how the people near you find their bearings. You have a name for doing it and the name leaves you out, and under the name is the point where what you notice connects to the ones around you.

What people who hold gatherings do is make the shared thing repeatable. Say the thing you know and feel, out loud, once, as if it were yours to say — no softening, no summary afterward. If it keeps coming up for someone, tell it again slower. What you'll have is the sound of your own voice as part of the room.
